title: Integrating Around a Job
hook: Grace's subscriber doesn't want Wednesday news on Friday. Both teams are hitting their numbers.
counterintuition: When every department meets its own target, the buyer's job can still break at the boundary between them. Despite appearances, local optimization is not coordination, and coordination is not integration.
tryThisNow: Name one internal decision from last month that improved one function's metric. Write a sentence on whether it made the buyer's progress easier or harder. If you cannot answer, no one was governing the tradeoff.
keyTakeaway: Integration around the job means one person or process governs the tradeoffs between functions so that each local win is tested against whether the buyer's full progress is protected.

breakdown.fastRead:
Grace's print and digital teams both hit their numbers this quarter. A subscriber calls to complain: the Wednesday property section she reads online is two weeks old by the time it posts. Both teams optimized their piece. Nobody governed the moment the subscriber hired the paper for: property news while it still matters.

This is the integration problem. When every department succeeds on its own metric, the buyer can still fail to get the job done. The job has to become the reference point across all the pieces, not just inside each one. Without a governing job, local wins add up to a buyer's loss.
breakdown.deepRead:
Coordination means people talk. Integration means someone governs tradeoffs by asking whether each local decision helps or hurts the buyer's full progress. Those are not the same thing.

At 7:38 a.m., Antoine's dispatch algorithm logs an 18 percent gain in delivery volume per courier-hour. Customer satisfaction scores fell the same week. The system optimized what the operations team measured. The clients hired the service to deliver time-sensitive documents with signature confirmation before 10 a.m. Two metrics. Two jobs. The algorithm served one and damaged the other because nobody was governing which job should win when they conflicted.

The allergy table in Giuliana's school cafeteria is clean, stocked, and certified. Safety protocols pass every inspection. A parent writes to say her son eats alone every day because none of his friends will sit there. Food services owned the safety job. The school's social environment job, belonging and learning together, was never coordinated into the same system of accountability. Two functions, each succeeding, with a gap between them that no one owned.

Integration requires naming the primary job the whole offering is hired for, then building a single accountability that crosses departmental lines. The job does not ask departments to stop having metrics. It asks that every metric be answerable to whether it helps or hurts the buyer's full progress. That is harder than a meeting. It requires someone to say, when your local win creates a gap in the buyer's path, your local win loses.

Local optimization is not coordination, and coordination is not integration.
breakdown.fullRead:
What happens when everyone does their job well? In most organizations, the answer is assumed to be obvious: the whole works. But the whole only works if the pieces were designed around the same reference point. When each piece was designed around its own metric, doing your job well can actively damage what the buyer hired.

This is the integration gap. It is not caused by failure. It is caused by partial optimization. The print team runs a P&L. The digital team runs a P&L. Both are rewarded for their own numbers. Nobody is rewarded for the moment the subscriber hired the newspaper to deliver: property news while it is still current, available in the format she chooses, on the day it matters. That moment lives in the gap between the two departments, and gaps are not managed by accident.

Jack is holding two documents at once: the plumber's as-built and the homeowner's tile pattern. The drain placement is correct per the plumber's scope. It is wrong for the tile layout the homeowner chose. Both contractors finished on time. Both delivered what they were hired for by their respective contracts. Nobody held the whole job: a functional, beautiful bathroom by move-in day. The homeowner is now absorbing the cost of coordinating two people who each did their work correctly. The integration gap is real, measurable, and it lives at the handoff.

Think about the last time a project went sideways even though each team delivered on time. Did anyone ask whether the handoffs between teams preserved the progress the buyer was trying to make? In most cases, the answer is no. The handoff is managed as a transfer of task, not a test of whether the buyer's job is still intact on the other side.

Hanna's transit agencies completed a genuine technical integration: three separate payment systems now speak to each other. It was expensive, it was slow, and it was celebrated internally. Six months later, cross-agency ridership in the overlap zone is flat. Exit surveys show riders still buying two day-passes because neither app shows combined journey time. The payment integration served the agencies' internal accounting job. It did not serve the rider's job: plan and execute an efficient multi-modal trip from one screen. The agencies coordinated. They did not integrate around the right job.

Hadiya's IT team completed every onboarding task within SLA. Hardware provisioned. Accounts created. Licenses assigned. Forty percent of new hires in the week-two survey still could not access the project management tool before their first team meeting. The access required a manager approval that IT does not own. The job (productive in team by week one) broke at the IT-to-manager boundary, not inside IT's scope. IT succeeded. The job failed. The boundary was unmanaged because the job was never the governing reference point across both functions.

Integration is a governance question, not just a coordination question. Governance means someone has authority to say: when your local optimization creates a gap in the buyer's progress, your optimization must change. Coordination without governance produces polite agreements that unravel at the first metric conflict.

The practical test: name the job the buyer hired, then trace the path to completed progress. Mark every handoff. At each handoff, ask whether someone is accountable for the job surviving the transfer. If the answer is no one, the job is unprotected at that boundary, and every local win on either side is provisional.

examples.title: Grace names the job the internal division is fracturing

planSpec.domain: regional newspaper (print and digital split P&L)
planSpec.stakes: two teams hit their numbers while the subscriber job breaks
planSpec.requiredBeat: both teams hitting their numbers while the subscriber job breaks at the boundary

examples.scenario: "Both teams are hitting their numbers," the publisher says, leaning back in the chair. Grace sets the subscriber complaint on the conference table. "Your Wednesday property section is two weeks old by the time I get the digital version." Print runs its own P&L. Digital runs its own. Neither is wrong on paper. Grace faces a choice: praise the quarterly results or name the job that the internal division is fracturing. The property editor is waiting on the phone for the verdict.
examples.whatToDo: Name the subscriber's job before discussing team metrics: timely property news in the format she chose. Map which boundary between print and digital caused the delay and assign a governing owner there.
examples.whyItMatters: Split P&Ls reward local performance and leave the boundary between them unmanaged. The job cannot survive a boundary no one owns.

examples.title: Antoine sees two metrics pointing at two different jobs

planSpec.stakes: volume optimization damages time-sensitive delivery job
planSpec.requiredBeat: efficiency gain and satisfaction drop reveal two metrics serving two different jobs

examples.scenario: At 7:38 a.m., Antoine reviews the dispatch dashboard. Efficiency per courier-hour is up 18 percent. He predicts a strong week. The client satisfaction report arrives at noon: scores fell. The algorithm routed for volume. The client's job is time-sensitive document delivery with signature confirmation before 10 a.m. The reveal is quiet and specific. Antoine must decide whether to attribute the gap to algorithm scope or to reconfigure what the dispatch system is being asked to optimize.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the two metrics by the job each serves. Ask which job the client hired the service to do, then make that job the constraint the algorithm must satisfy before optimizing anything else.
examples.whyItMatters: Two metrics measuring two different jobs will always conflict. The job that pays the client's contract should govern, not the one that is easier to track.

examples.title: Giuliana finds the allergy table clean and her student eating alone

planSpec.stakes: safety job and belonging job never coordinated
planSpec.requiredBeat: safety protocols pass while the belonging job breaks at the organizational boundary

examples.scenario: The allergy table smells of sanitizer and fresh fruit, every item labeled, every surface certified. Giuliana checks the safety log. Everything passes. A parent's note is clipped to the folder above the log: "My son eats alone every day because none of his friends will sit at the allergy table." Food services optimized for safety. The school's social environment, belonging and learning together, was never coordinated into the same accountability structure. Two jobs, two departments, no one governing the gap. Giuliana must decide whether to flag the coordination gap to the principal or absorb it as a food services redesign problem.
examples.whatToDo: Name both jobs explicitly: physical safety and social belonging. Assign someone to govern the boundary between food services and student life, with authority to require changes when one job breaks the other.
examples.whyItMatters: Two functions can each succeed on their own terms while a student pays the cost of the unmanaged gap between them. Integration requires the boundary to be owned.

examples.title: Jack holds the as-built and the tile pattern at the same time

planSpec.domain: home renovation contractor handoff (plumber to tile subcontractor)
planSpec.stakes: both contractors succeeded; nobody held the whole job
planSpec.requiredBeat: technically correct drain placement is wrong for the tile pattern; nobody held the whole bathroom job

examples.scenario: You are holding the plumber's as-built in one hand and the homeowner's tile pattern in the other. The drain is placed exactly where the spec said to put it. The tile pattern the homeowner chose requires a centered drain. Both contractors delivered their scopes on time and on budget. Neither was wrong on paper. You are about to decide whether to absorb the coordination cost now, before the tile goes down, or let the handoff complete and send the problem forward. The homeowner moves in on Friday.
examples.whatToDo: Stop the handoff before the tile goes down. Name the whole job: a functional, beautiful bathroom by move-in day. Assign that job as the governing reference for the scope conflict. The coordination cost now is cheaper than a floor tear-out.
examples.whyItMatters: Correct individual scopes do not guarantee the whole job survives the handoff. Someone has to hold the full job across contractors, or the buyer pays for the gap.

examples.title: Hanna reads flat ridership after the payment integration celebrated

planSpec.stakes: agencies integrated the wrong job and left the rider job unserved
planSpec.requiredBeat: payment integration served internal accounting; rider job of planning a multi-modal trip remained broken

examples.scenario: Hanna pulls the six-month ridership report and sets it beside the launch press release. The three-agency payment integration was technically successful. Cross-agency ridership in the overlap zone is flat. Exit surveys are plain: riders still buy two day-passes because neither app shows combined journey time. Payment integration served the agencies' accounting job. The rider's job, plan and execute an efficient multi-modal trip, was never integrated around.
examples.whatToDo: Restate the rider's job and test every integration decision against it. Combined journey time visibility is not a feature request; it is the integration the agencies did not build because they governed by their own accounting job.
examples.whyItMatters: Technical integration between systems can miss the buyer's job entirely if the governing question is internal efficiency instead of the rider's full progress.

examples.title: Hadiya traces the gap to the IT-to-manager boundary

planSpec.domain: corporate IT onboarding for new employees
planSpec.stakes: IT completed its scope; the job broke at the boundary IT does not own
planSpec.requiredBeat: IT completed within SLA; job broke at IT-to-manager boundary IT does not own

examples.scenario: Hadiya reviews the week-two onboarding survey. IT completed every task within SLA: hardware, accounts, licenses, access to company drives. Forty percent of new employees still could not access the project management tool before their first team meeting. The tool requires a manager approval step. IT does not own that step. The job, productive in team by week one, broke at the boundary between IT and the hiring manager, not inside IT's scope. IT's SLA was met. The job was not. Hadiya must decide whether to close the ticket as complete or reopen the process to include the manager approval step in the onboarding definition.
examples.whatToDo: Map the onboarding path to the job, not to departmental handoffs. Assign a single owner who is accountable for the job surviving every transfer, including the IT-to-manager step IT cannot control alone.
examples.whyItMatters: SLA completion inside one department does not protect a job that crosses multiple departments. The job needs a governing owner at every boundary, not just a checklist inside each scope.

questions.prompt: A print team and a digital team both hit their quarterly revenue targets. A subscriber complains that the digital property section is two weeks out of date. What does this situation most clearly illustrate?
choices: Local optimization by each team can break the buyer's job at the boundary between departments.
The subscriber is comparing the product against a competitor with faster publishing cycles.
Quarterly revenue is the correct signal for whether a buyer's job is being served.
questions.explanation: Both teams succeeded on their own metrics while the subscriber's job, timely property news, broke at the boundary between them. Meeting internal targets does not guarantee the buyer's progress is protected.

questions.prompt: A dispatch algorithm increases delivery volume per courier-hour by 18 percent. Client satisfaction scores fall the same week. Which question should the operations manager ask first?
choices: Which courier had the most complaints this week?
Which job was the algorithm governing, and is that the job the client hired the service to do?
Is the 18 percent gain large enough to offset the satisfaction drop in the next client contract review?
questions.explanation: Two metrics serving two different jobs will always conflict. The question is which job the client hired for, and whether the optimization served that job or a different internal one.

questions.prompt: A school's allergy accommodations pass every safety inspection. A parent reports her child eats alone daily because friends will not sit at the allergy table. Which diagnosis is most accurate?
choices: Food services and the student life function each succeeded on their own terms while the boundary between them went unmanaged.
The safety protocols are insufficient and need to be revised to include social accommodations.
Parents are setting expectations that go beyond what a school is hired to provide.
questions.explanation: Safety and belonging are two separate jobs, each owned by a different function. Neither failed within its own scope. The integration gap is the unmanaged boundary between them.

questions.prompt: A plumber places a drain correctly per spec. A tile subcontractor arrives and finds the drain is in the wrong position for the tile pattern the homeowner chose. Both contractors finished on time. What is the root cause of the problem?
choices: The tile subcontractor should have reviewed the plumber's as-built before the job started.
No one held the whole job across contractors, so a technically correct local scope created a defect in the buyer's full progress.
The homeowner made a tile pattern choice that was incompatible with standard drain placement.
questions.explanation: Each contractor succeeded inside their own scope. The integration gap is the absence of anyone governing the full job across the handoff between them.

questions.prompt: Three transit agencies integrate their payment systems. Six months later, cross-agency ridership is flat. Exit surveys show riders still buy two separate day-passes. What should the postmortem conclude?
choices: The payment integration was not technically complete and needs another phase.
Rider behavior is slow to change and the results should be measured over a longer period.
The integration served the agencies' internal accounting job rather than the rider's job of planning a multi-modal trip.
questions.explanation: Technical success between systems can miss the buyer's job entirely when the governing question is internal efficiency over the rider's full progress. The right job was never used as the integration target.

questions.prompt: IT completes onboarding within SLA. Forty percent of new employees cannot access the project management tool before their first team meeting because it requires a manager approval step IT does not own. What should the response be?
choices: Assign a governing owner for the onboarding job who is accountable across the IT-to-manager boundary, not just within IT's scope.

Revise the SLA definition: the current SLA was set without including the manager approval step, so the measurement boundary is incorrect rather than the accountability structure, and if the SLA is rewritten to include driving manager approvals to completion within the onboarding window, IT gains the right metrics to track the full job without requiring a new governance role or a structural change to authority lines.

Automating the manager approval step removes the governance gap by eliminating the handoff: if the system sends the manager a one-click approval request immediately after IT completes its tasks and escalates after 24 hours, the manual dependency disappears without requiring anyone to govern across boundaries, because the technology makes the cross-boundary coordination happen without human coordination overhead.
questions.explanation: The job broke at a boundary IT does not own. Adding SLA measures to IT for steps IT cannot control does not fix the integration gap. The fix is governance across the boundary.

questions.prompt: A manager says her team has weekly cross-functional meetings where all departments are represented. Buyers still report that their job breaks at handoffs. What does this situation reveal about the difference between coordination and integration?
choices: The meetings are working but participants lack sufficient authority: the departments attend but cannot commit resources or override their own function's policies in real time, so each meeting produces only provisional agreements that require separate approval, and elevating the meeting to include department heads with budget authority would give the coordination structure the decision-making power it needs to resolve handoff failures before they reach buyers.
Coordination means people talk; integration means someone governs tradeoffs by testing whether the buyer's job survives each handoff.

The buyer reports are a lagging indicator and the meetings are functioning as designed: cross-functional familiarity takes twelve to eighteen months to translate into smooth handoffs because teams need to learn each other's constraints through repeated interaction, and the current handoff failures are a transitional phase rather than a structural problem requiring a new governance mechanism.
questions.explanation: Coordination and integration are different. Coordination creates shared information. Integration requires a governing authority that can require local changes when they damage the buyer's full progress.

questions.prompt: A team is proposing a new efficiency initiative that will reduce costs in one department by 12 percent. Before approving it, what is the integration test?
choices: Whether the 12 percent saving is large enough to offset any buyer dissatisfaction.
Whether the savings can be shared across departments to avoid internal resentment.
Whether the local efficiency gain helps or hurts the buyer's full progress across all handoffs.
questions.explanation: The integration test asks whether the local win serves or damages the buyer's job across the full path, not whether the saving is large enough to justify a tradeoff.

questions.prompt: Every department in a product organization reports that its metrics are green this quarter. The CEO wants to know whether this means the buyer's job is being protected. What analysis distinguishes local success from integration success?
choices: All-green departmental metrics are sufficient evidence of organizational health: if every function is meeting its defined performance standard, the system is operating correctly by definition, and the CEO should look for a specific metric that is not green rather than questioning the entire measurement framework, because well-designed metrics capture the outcomes the organization is responsible for.

The right analysis is a customer satisfaction trend: if NPS or satisfaction scores are stable or rising alongside green departmental metrics, the buyer's job is being protected, and if satisfaction is falling while department metrics are green, the divergence pinpoints which handoff is failing because it names the customer segment experiencing the problem at the point where the metrics and the experience diverge.
Trace the buyer's path from first contact to completed progress, and test whether someone is accountable for the job surviving every handoff between departments.
questions.explanation: Green internal metrics do not guarantee the buyer's job is protected. Integration success requires a path analysis that checks whether the job survives each boundary, not just whether each department reported a good quarter.

reviewCards.front: Every department hit its target. A buyer still failed. What is the first question?
reviewCards.back: Ask where the buyer's progress broke. The failure is almost always at a boundary between functions, not inside any single department's scope. Identify which handoff was unmanaged.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between coordination and integration?
reviewCards.back: Coordination means people share information across functions. Integration means someone governs tradeoffs by testing whether the buyer's job survives every handoff. Only one of these protects the job when departments conflict.

reviewCards.front: Two departments each succeed on their own metrics. The buyer's job breaks. Where do you assign governance?
reviewCards.back: Assign governance at the boundary between the two departments, not inside either one. The governing owner needs authority to require changes from both functions when the buyer's full progress is at risk.

reviewCards.front: A technical integration between systems is technically complete. Buyers are not using it. What does the postmortem ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask which job the integration was built to serve. If it served an internal accounting or operational goal, not the buyer's progress, technical completeness is irrelevant to adoption.

reviewCards.front: What is the practical integration test before approving a local efficiency initiative?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the efficiency gain helps or hurts the buyer's full progress across all handoffs. A local win that creates a gap in the buyer's path is not an improvement to the offering, regardless of the departmental savings.

implementationPlan.title: Governing the Job Across Departmental Boundaries
implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is governing the job across departmental boundaries, not just inside each function. Trace the buyer's full path, mark every handoff, and assign accountability for the job surviving each transfer.

ifThenPlans.plan: If every department reports a win and a buyer still complains, then map the handoffs between functions and find the boundary where no one is governing the buyer's progress.
If a health routine is technically correct at each step but not producing progress, then trace which handoff between steps is unmanaged and assign yourself the governing responsibility there.
If a project involves multiple people each doing their part, then name the whole job in writing and check that someone is accountable for it at every transfer point.

If a shared task keeps breaking despite everyone doing their assigned part, then hold a meeting where the job is named first and each person's role is evaluated by whether it helps the whole job, not just their portion.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, trace one buyer path that crosses at least two internal departments. Write each handoff point, name who owns the job at each boundary, and mark any boundary where no one is currently governing whether the buyer's progress survives.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review one recent initiative that succeeded internally. Ask whether it improved or damaged the buyer's full progress across every handoff. If you cannot answer the question, identify who should be able to.

memorableLines.text: Local optimization is not coordination, and coordination is not integration.
memorableLines.why: It draws the three-level distinction that most teams collapse into one word.

memorableLines.text: Two metrics. Two jobs. The algorithm served one and damaged the other because nobody was governing which job should win when they conflicted.
memorableLines.why: It makes the integration gap concrete and names the missing governance.

memorableLines.text: gaps are not managed by accident.
memorableLines.why: It is the shortest statement of why integration requires deliberate ownership.
